title: Japanese Food Guide for First-Timers
excerpt: Japan is a food lover's paradise. Here's an overview of what to eat, how dining works, and how to navigate Japanese food as a first-time visitor.
content:
Japan is one of the world's great food destinations, and eating well here is effortless — even on a budget. For first-timers, the variety can be exciting and a little intimidating, so here's the big-picture overview of what to eat and how dining works.

The range of Japanese food

Japanese cuisine goes far beyond sushi. You'll find ramen (rich noodle soups), sushi and sashimi, tempura (light battered fryups), udon and soba noodles, tonkatsu (breaded pork cutlet), yakitori (grilled skewers), donburi (rice bowls), okonomiyaki and takoyaki (savory specialties), curry rice, and refined kaiseki multi-course meals. Regional specialties abound, so eating your way across the country is part of the adventure.

Where to eat

Options span every budget: humble ramen counters and standing noodle bars, lively izakaya (Japanese pubs) for small plates and drinks, specialty restaurants focused on a single dish, department store food halls (depachika), bustling food markets, and surprisingly excellent convenience stores for quick, cheap meals. You're never far from something good.

How dining works

  • Many restaurants have plastic food models or photo menus in the window, making ordering easy even without Japanese.
  • Some places use ticket machines — buy a meal ticket at the machine, hand it to staff.
  • You'll often get a hot or cold towel (oshibori) to clean your hands.
  • Say "itadakimasu" before eating if you like (a customary phrase of thanks).
  • No tipping — ever.

Etiquette basics

  • It's fine — even appreciated — to slurp noodles.
  • Don't stick chopsticks upright in rice or pass food chopstick-to-chopstick (both have funerary associations).
  • Pour drinks for others rather than yourself in social settings.
  • Try not to eat while walking.

For picky eaters and dietary needs

Japan is easy for many eaters — rice, noodles, grilled meats, and familiar items are everywhere. Strict vegetarians, vegans, and those with allergies need more care, as dashi (fish stock) and hidden ingredients are common; it's worth learning a few phrases or carrying a translation card (covered in our dietary guide).

Drinks

Beyond food, try sake (rice wine), Japanese beer and whisky, shochu, and the ubiquitous green tea and matcha. Vending machines everywhere dispense hot and cold drinks, and tap water is safe to drink.

Bottom line

From a ¥500 bowl of ramen to a multi-course kaiseki feast, Japan delivers extraordinary food at every level. Be adventurous, use photo menus and ticket machines without fear, mind a few etiquette basics, and let eating be one of the highlights of your trip.

title: How to Order and Eat in Japan
excerpt: Ticket machines, plastic food models, and no tipping — here's how ordering and eating actually works in Japanese restaurants, step by step.
content:
Ordering food in Japan is easier than first-timers fear, even without speaking Japanese — the systems are designed to be visual and efficient. Here's how dining actually works, from walking in to paying up.

Finding a place to eat

Look for restaurants with plastic food models or photo menus in the window — a Japanese institution that makes choosing easy. Many specialize in one thing (ramen, tonkatsu, sushi), which usually means they do it well. Department store food floors and station areas are reliable for variety.

Getting seated

At many places you seat yourself or wait to be shown to a seat; at counters you often just sit down. Staff may greet you with "irasshaimase" (welcome). Hold up fingers to indicate your party size if there's a language gap.

Ordering methods

Ticket machines

Many ramen and casual spots use a ticket vending machine near the entrance: insert cash (some take cards), press the button for your dish (often with photos), collect the ticket, and hand it to staff. No conversation needed.

Photo and picture menus

Point at what you want on a photo menu — universally understood. Some restaurants have English menus or tablets; many now have QR-code menus you scan at the table.

Call-button service

Some restaurants, especially izakaya and family chains, have a call button on the table to summon staff when you're ready, rather than them hovering.

While you eat

  • You'll usually receive a wet towel (oshibori) to clean your hands — use it for hands, not your face.
  • Water or tea is often free and self-serve or brought automatically.
  • At izakaya you may be served a small dish (otoshi) you didn't order — it's a normal seating charge.
  • Slurping noodles is fine.
  • Don't stick chopsticks upright in rice or pass food chopstick-to-chopstick.

Paying

  • You usually pay at the front counter, not at the table — bring your bill or ticket stub to the register.
  • Cash is always accepted; cards increasingly so, but carry cash for small places.
  • There's a small tray for your money/card — place it there rather than handing it over.
  • No tipping — the total is the total.

A few useful phrases

  • Sumimasen — "excuse me" (to get attention).
  • Kore o kudasai — "this one, please" (while pointing).
  • Oishii — "delicious."
  • Gochisousama — said after a meal, a thanks for the food.

Bottom line

Between ticket machines, photo menus, and pay-at-the-counter simplicity, ordering in Japan rarely requires much language at all. Relax, point confidently, slurp your noodles, and skip the tip — you'll dine like a local in no time.

title: Vegetarian and Dietary Needs in Japan
excerpt: Vegetarian, vegan, or have allergies? Japanese food has hidden fish stock and ingredients. Here's how to navigate dietary needs as a traveler.
content:
Japan is a wonderful food destination, but travelers with dietary restrictions need to plan a bit more carefully than elsewhere. Vegetarian, vegan, and allergy-conscious eating is very doable, but hidden ingredients are common. Here's how to navigate it.

The hidden-ingredient challenge

The biggest surprise for vegetarians and vegans is dashi — a stock made from fish (bonito) and/or seaweed — which forms the base of countless dishes, including many that seem vegetable-based like miso soup, broths, and sauces. Pork, fish flakes, and meat-based broths also appear in unexpected places. "Vegetable" dishes are often not strictly vegetarian by Western standards.

Strategies that work

  • Learn key phrases or carry a card. A translation card explaining your restrictions (in Japanese) is invaluable — state clearly what you can't eat, including dashi/fish stock for strict vegetarians.
  • Seek out specialist food. Shojin ryori (Buddhist temple cuisine) is traditionally vegan and available near some temples — a delicious, safe option. Indian and other international restaurants also offer reliable vegetarian choices.
  • Use dedicated apps and guides. Vegetarian/vegan restaurant-finder resources have grown a lot and help locate suitable places, especially in big cities.
  • Stick to clearly safe items when unsure — plain rice, certain noodles (check broth), tempura vegetables, tofu dishes (confirm no dashi), fruit, and convenience-store items with checkable labels.

Allergies

For food allergies, extra caution is essential, as cross-contamination and hidden ingredients (soy, wheat, fish, shellfish, egg) are common and language barriers complicate communication. Carry a clear, detailed allergy card in Japanese, research in advance, and when in doubt, choose simpler dishes where you can verify ingredients. Severe allergy sufferers should be especially careful and may want to consult specific resources before traveling.

Vegan-specific notes

Veganism is less common in Japan, so awareness varies. Beyond shojin ryori and dedicated vegan spots (increasingly found in cities), you'll need to check for dashi, egg, and dairy carefully. Big cities like Tokyo and Kyoto have a growing vegan scene; rural areas are harder.

Halal and other needs

Halal options are growing, especially in tourist areas and major cities, with some certified restaurants and prayer facilities — research ahead, as availability is limited outside urban centers. Gluten-free is also challenging given soy sauce (which contains wheat) and other staples; carry a card and verify.

Practical tips

  • Big cities are far easier than rural areas — plan special meals where options are richer.
  • Convenience stores and supermarkets let you check labels (a translation app helps).
  • Department store food halls offer variety where you can inspect items.
  • Communicate restrictions clearly and politely; staff are generally helpful when they understand.

Bottom line

With preparation — a good translation card, knowledge of hidden dashi, and a list of suitable spots — vegetarians, vegans, and allergy-conscious travelers can eat well in Japan. Lean on shojin ryori, international options, and the big-city scene, and verify ingredients when unsure.

title: Ramen Types Explained: A Guide for First-Timers
excerpt: Shoyu, miso, shio, tonkotsu — Japanese ramen comes in many styles. Here's what each one is and how to order your perfect bowl.
content:
Ramen is one of Japan's great food joys — a steaming bowl of noodles in rich broth, endlessly varied by region and shop. For first-timers, the styles can be confusing, so here's a guide to the main types and how to order.

The four classic broth styles

Shoyu (soy sauce)

Shoyu ramen has a soy-sauce-based broth — savory, clear, and brown-tinted. It's one of the original and most common styles, balanced and approachable. A great default for first-timers.

Miso

Miso ramen uses fermented soybean paste for a hearty, rich, slightly sweet broth. Originating in cold Hokkaido, it's warming and full-bodied — excellent in cooler weather.

Shio (salt)

Shio ramen is salt-based, the lightest and often clearest broth, letting the underlying flavors shine. Delicate and refreshing compared to richer styles.

Tonkotsu (pork bone)

Tonkotsu ramen features a broth made by simmering pork bones for hours into a creamy, milky, intensely rich soup. A specialty of Kyushu (Hakata style), it's a favorite for its deep flavor. Note: tonkotsu refers to the pork-bone broth, distinct from the seasoning.

The noodles and toppings

Noodles vary from thin and straight to thick and wavy, often matched to the broth. Common toppings include chashu (braised pork slices), a soft-boiled marinated egg (ajitama), green onions, bamboo shoots (menma), nori seaweed, and corn or butter in some regional styles. Many shops let you customize richness, noodle firmness, and toppings.

How to order

  • Many ramen shops use a ticket machine — pick your bowl (photos help), pay, hand the ticket to staff.
  • Some ask your preferences: noodle firmness, broth richness, oil level — when unsure, choose the standard.
  • At chains like Ichiran, you order via a form, ideal for solo diners in private booths.
  • Add extras like an egg or extra chashu if offered.

Eating etiquette

  • Slurping is encouraged — it cools the noodles and is considered appreciative.
  • Eat promptly while hot; noodles soften quickly.
  • Use the renge (spoon) for broth and the chopsticks for noodles.
  • It's fine to lift the bowl to drink the broth.

Regional ramen to seek out

Ramen is deeply regional: Hakata/Kyushu tonkotsu, Sapporo miso, Tokyo shoyu, and countless local variations. Trying a region's signature ramen is a delicious way to experience local food culture as you travel.

Bottom line

Start with shoyu or tonkotsu if you're unsure, slurp away, and explore regional styles as you go. A great bowl of ramen is one of Japan's most satisfying and affordable pleasures — and there's a style for every taste.

title: Sushi Guide for Beginners
excerpt: From conveyor-belt spots to high-end counters, here's how to enjoy sushi in Japan — the types, the etiquette, and how to order.
content:
Sushi in Japan is a revelation — fresher, more varied, and often cheaper than what you may know from home. From cheap conveyor-belt spots to refined counters, here's how to enjoy it as a beginner.

Know the basic types

  • Nigiri: a slice of fish (or other topping) over a small mound of vinegared rice — the classic.
  • Maki: rolled sushi with rice and fillings wrapped in seaweed, cut into pieces.
  • Sashimi: slices of raw fish served without rice (technically not sushi, but often alongside).
  • Gunkan: "battleship" sushi with a seaweed wrap holding soft toppings like roe.
  • Temaki: hand-rolled cones.

Common toppings include tuna (maguro), salmon (sake), shrimp (ebi), eel (unagi), egg (tamago), and many seasonal fish.

Where to eat sushi

Conveyor-belt sushi (kaiten-zushi)

Fun, cheap, and beginner-friendly: plates circulate on a belt (or arrive via touchscreen order), color-coded by price. Grab what looks good or order from a tablet. Great for families and the budget-conscious, and a low-pressure way to try lots of types.

Standard sushi restaurants

Mid-range spots offer sets and à la carte in a relaxed setting, often with picture menus — a comfortable middle ground.

High-end sushi counters

For a special experience, an omakase (chef's choice) meal at a counter is sublime, with the chef serving pieces one by one. These can be expensive and may require reservations, but they're a culinary highlight.

How to eat sushi properly

  • Nigiri can be eaten by hand or with chopsticks — both are acceptable.
  • Dip the fish side (not the rice) lightly in soy sauce to avoid it falling apart and oversalting.
  • Eat each piece in one bite if you can.
  • Ginger (gari) is a palate cleanser between pieces, not a topping.
  • Use a little wasabi, but note good sushi is often already seasoned — taste first.
  • Don't drown sushi in soy sauce or mix wasabi into it at high-end places.

Ordering tips

  • At conveyor spots, watch the color-coded plates for pricing and stack them to be tallied at the end.
  • At counters, you can ask the chef for recommendations or go omakase.
  • Green tea is usually free and self-serve (powder + hot water tap).
  • No tipping, as always.

Bottom line

Whether you start with affordable conveyor-belt plates or splurge on an omakase counter, sushi in Japan is unmissable. Dip the fish not the rice, eat in one bite, cleanse with ginger, and savor some of the freshest seafood you'll ever taste.

title: Must-Try Japanese Dishes for First-Timers
excerpt: Beyond sushi and ramen — here are the essential Japanese dishes every first-time visitor should try, from tempura to okonomiyaki.
content:
Japanese cuisine is vast, and a first trip is the perfect excuse to eat widely. Beyond the famous sushi and ramen, here are the essential dishes to seek out — a hit list to make sure you taste the best of Japan.

Noodles

  • Ramen: noodle soup in rich broth — the everyday favorite, with regional styles to explore.
  • Udon: thick, chewy wheat noodles in broth, comforting and mild.
  • Soba: thin buckwheat noodles, served hot in broth or cold with dipping sauce.

Rice dishes

  • Donburi: rice bowls topped with various ingredients — gyudon (beef), katsudon (pork cutlet), oyakodon (chicken and egg).
  • Curry rice: Japan's beloved, mild-sweet curry over rice — hearty comfort food.
  • Onigiri: rice balls with fillings, a perfect cheap snack (convenience stores excel at these).

Fried and grilled

  • Tempura: seafood and vegetables in a light, crisp batter.
  • Tonkatsu: a breaded, deep-fried pork cutlet, usually with shredded cabbage and rice.
  • Yakitori: skewered grilled chicken (and other parts), an izakaya staple.
  • Gyoza: pan-fried dumplings, crisp on the bottom.
  • Karaage: Japanese fried chicken — juicy and addictive.

Regional savory specialties

  • Okonomiyaki: a savory pancake of cabbage and batter with various fillings, topped with sauce and mayo — big in Osaka and Hiroshima.
  • Takoyaki: ball-shaped snacks filled with octopus, an Osaka street-food icon.
  • Sukiyaki and shabu-shabu: hot-pot dishes where you cook thin meat and vegetables at the table.
  • Yakiniku: Japanese-style grilled meat you cook yourself.

Refined and traditional

  • Kaiseki: an elegant multi-course meal of seasonal dishes — a special-occasion experience, often at ryokan.
  • Unagi: grilled freshwater eel glazed with sweet sauce over rice.
  • Sashimi: pristine slices of raw fish.

Sweets and snacks

  • Matcha sweets: green-tea desserts, especially around Kyoto.
  • Mochi and wagashi: traditional Japanese confections.
  • Taiyaki and dorayaki: fish-shaped and pancake-style treats with sweet fillings.
  • Convenience-store desserts: surprisingly excellent and cheap.

Don't forget the drinks

Pair your meals with sake, Japanese beer or whisky, shochu, or green tea and matcha. Vending machines everywhere offer hot and cold options.

Bottom line

Make a list and eat your way through it — Japan rewards culinary curiosity at every price point. From a convenience-store onigiri to a kaiseki feast, trying these dishes is one of the most delicious parts of any first trip.

title: Japanese Convenience Store Food Guide
excerpt: Japan's konbini are a budget traveler's secret weapon — cheap, delicious, 24/7 food. Here's what to buy and why konbini are so good.
content:
One of the happiest surprises for first-time visitors is how astonishingly good Japan's convenience stores (konbini) are. Far beyond gas-station snacks, they offer cheap, fresh, genuinely tasty food around the clock — a budget traveler's best friend. Here's what to know.

Why konbini are amazing

Japanese convenience stores — the big chains are everywhere, including in train stations — are clean, ubiquitous, and stocked with quality food at low prices. They're open 24/7, accept IC cards and cash, and are a reliable source of meals, snacks, and travel essentials. For cheap eating without sacrificing quality, they're unbeatable.

What to buy

Onigiri (rice balls)

Triangular rice balls wrapped in seaweed with fillings like salmon, tuna-mayo, or pickled plum. Cheap, filling, and a perfect grab-and-go meal or snack. The clever packaging keeps the seaweed crisp until you open it.

Bento and ready meals

Boxed bento meals and hot dishes can be heated in-store by staff — a full, balanced meal for a few dollars. Pasta, rice bowls, and noodle dishes are all available.

Sandwiches

The famous egg salad sandwich (tamago sando) has a cult following, along with fruit sandwiches and other neatly packaged options.

Hot snacks at the counter

Many konbini have a hot case with fried chicken (the famous karaage), steamed buns (nikuman), corn dogs, and other warm snacks — point and order.

Noodles and soups

Instant cup noodles (add hot water from the in-store dispenser) and fresh-ish noodle bowls are cheap and satisfying.

Drinks and sweets

  • A huge range of hot and cold drinks — coffee, teas, juices, sports drinks.
  • Fresh-brewed convenience-store coffee from a machine, surprisingly good and cheap.
  • Excellent desserts — puddings, cakes, mochi, ice cream — that rival dedicated shops.

Beyond food

Konbini also sell travel essentials: toiletries, umbrellas, phone chargers, socks, basic medicine, and more. Many have ATMs that accept foreign cards (the 7-Eleven ATMs are reliable for withdrawals), clean restrooms, and bill-payment services. They're genuine lifesavers on the road.

Tips

  • Staff will heat your meal and provide utensils and chopsticks — just ask or it's often automatic.
  • There may be a small eat-in area, but generally avoid eating while walking; find a spot to stand or sit.
  • Pay with your IC card for speed.
  • Stock up on breakfast or late-night snacks when restaurants are closed.

Bottom line

Don't sleep on konbini — they're one of the best things about traveling in Japan. Cheap, delicious, and everywhere, they make eating well on a budget effortless. At least once, build a meal entirely from a convenience store; you'll be impressed.

title: Where to Eat in Tokyo: Best Areas and Food Experiences
excerpt: Tokyo is one of the world's greatest food cities. Here's where to eat — the best districts, market, and food experiences for visitors.
content:
Tokyo is arguably the world's greatest food city, with more top-rated restaurants than anywhere and incredible eating at every price point. For visitors, the challenge is choosing. Here's where to eat and the food experiences not to miss.

Tsukiji Outer Market

The Tsukiji Outer Market is a must for food lovers — a warren of stalls and small eateries serving fresh seafood, sushi, street snacks, and kitchen goods. Go in the morning for the freshest experience and a memorable seafood breakfast or lunch. It's one of Tokyo's great food destinations.

Best areas for dining

  • Shinjuku: everything from the atmospheric alley eateries of Omoide Yokocho to high-end restaurants and izakaya. A top all-round dining district.
  • Shibuya: trendy restaurants, izakaya, and cafes popular with a younger crowd.
  • Ginza: upscale dining, sushi counters, and department store food halls — the place to splurge.
  • Asakusa: traditional eats and street snacks around Senso-ji.
  • Ebisu and Nakameguro: known among locals for excellent restaurants and a stylish, lower-key scene.

Food experiences to seek out

  • Izakaya hopping: the quintessential Tokyo night — small plates and drinks at Japanese pubs.
  • Ramen: Tokyo has countless famous shops; try a classic shoyu bowl or a specialty spot.
  • Sushi: from conveyor-belt spots to refined omakase counters.
  • Depachika: the basement food halls of department stores, packed with gourmet takeaway and beautiful sweets.
  • Themed cafes and dessert spots: a fun, only-in-Tokyo novelty.

Tips for eating in Tokyo

  • Many of the best small restaurants seat only a handful — be ready to queue or go off-peak.
  • Lunch sets at nice restaurants offer great value versus dinner.
  • Look for places specializing in one dish — they usually excel at it.
  • Carry cash for tiny spots; izakaya may add a small seating charge (otoshi).
  • No tipping, ever.

Booking and tours

For high-end or very popular restaurants, reservations help (some require them). Food tours — through markets, izakaya districts, or street-food areas — are a great way for first-timers to eat well and learn, and are worth booking in advance.

Bottom line

From a market seafood breakfast to izakaya small plates to a splurge sushi counter, Tokyo delivers world-class food everywhere you turn. Pick a district, follow your appetite, and don't be afraid of the tiny specialist spots — that's where the magic often is.

title: Where to Eat in Kyoto: Best Areas and Local Specialties
excerpt: Kyoto's refined cuisine ranges from kaiseki to street snacks. Here's where to eat, from Nishiki Market to Pontocho Alley, and the local specialties to try.
content:
Kyoto's food culture is refined and deeply traditional, shaped by its imperial history and Buddhist heritage. From elegant multi-course meals to market snacks, here's where to eat and what makes Kyoto's cuisine special.

Nishiki Market

Nishiki Market — "Kyoto's Kitchen" — is a long covered arcade of food stalls and specialty shops selling local ingredients, pickles, sweets, seafood, and street snacks. It's a sensory delight and a perfect place to graze your way through Kyoto's flavors. A must for food lovers.

Pontocho Alley

Pontocho is a narrow, atmospheric lane running alongside the river, packed with restaurants ranging from affordable to high-end. Lantern-lit and traditional, it's one of the most magical places to have dinner in Kyoto, especially in the warmer months when some restaurants set up riverside platforms.

Kyoto's local specialties

  • Kaiseki: Kyoto is the home of this elegant multi-course cuisine of seasonal, artful dishes — a special-occasion splurge, often at ryokan or dedicated restaurants.
  • Yudofu: simmered tofu, a Kyoto specialty tied to its Buddhist temple cuisine — simple and delicate, often served near temple areas.
  • Shojin ryori: Buddhist vegetarian temple cuisine, refined and entirely plant-based.
  • Obanzai: traditional Kyoto home-style cooking of seasonal local dishes.
  • Matcha everything: green-tea sweets, desserts, and drinks abound — Kyoto and nearby Uji are matcha country.

Best areas for dining

  • Downtown (Kawaramachi/Pontocho/Gion): the densest concentration of restaurants, from casual to refined.
  • Gion: traditional dining and teahouses, atmospheric but often pricier.
  • Near Kyoto Station: plenty of options including a dining floor in the station complex.
  • Arashiyama: tofu specialists and scenic spots.

Tips for eating in Kyoto

  • Kaiseki and top restaurants often need reservations — book ahead, especially in peak seasons.
  • Lunch sets offer a more affordable taste of high-end Kyoto cuisine.
  • Try a tea house or matcha cafe for the full Kyoto experience.
  • Some traditional restaurants have set seatings and etiquette — read the details.
  • No tipping.

Food experiences

Consider a tea ceremony, a Nishiki Market food tour, or a kaiseki dinner for a deeper dive into Kyoto's culinary traditions. These experiences are popular and worth booking in advance.

Bottom line

Kyoto rewards a more contemplative approach to eating — graze Nishiki Market, dine along atmospheric Pontocho, and try local specialties like yudofu, kaiseki, and matcha sweets. It's a refined, seasonal food culture that's a highlight of any visit.

title: Izakaya Guide: How to Enjoy a Japanese Pub
excerpt: The izakaya is Japan's beloved pub — small plates, drinks, and a lively atmosphere. Here's how they work and how to enjoy one as a visitor.
content:
The izakaya is one of the best and most authentic ways to eat and drink in Japan — a casual Japanese pub serving an array of small plates alongside beer, sake, and other drinks, in a lively, social atmosphere. Here's how they work and how to make the most of one.

What an izakaya is

Think of an izakaya as a Japanese gastropub or tapas bar: you order a series of small dishes to share over drinks, rather than a single main course. The vibe is relaxed and convivial, ideal for groups or a solo diner at the counter. They range from cheap chains to refined specialist spots, and they're where locals unwind after work.

How it works

  • You'll often be seated and given a hot/cold towel (oshibori) and a menu.
  • An otoshi — a small appetizer you didn't order — is typically served; it's a normal seating/cover charge, not a scam.
  • Order a drink first (it's customary to start with a drink, often beer), then a few dishes to begin.
  • Order in rounds as you go, rather than all at once — that's the rhythm of an izakaya.
  • Use the call button on the table, if present, to summon staff.

What to order

  • Yakitori: grilled chicken skewers, an izakaya staple.
  • Edamame: salted soybeans, the classic starter.
  • Karaage: Japanese fried chicken.
  • Sashimi: fresh raw fish.
  • Gyoza: pan-fried dumplings.
  • Grilled fish, tofu dishes, pickles, salads, and fries — share a variety.

Drinks

Start with a beer ("nama biru" for draft) or try sake, shochu, a highball (whisky and soda, very popular), or chu-hai (fruity canned-style cocktails). It's polite to pour for others and let them pour for you. A toast of "kanpai!" kicks things off.

Etiquette and tips

  • The otoshi charge is normal — don't be surprised by it.
  • No tipping — the bill is the bill.
  • Some izakaya have all-you-can-drink (nomihodai) deals for a set time.
  • It can get smoky in older establishments, though smoking rules have tightened.
  • Pay at the counter or table depending on the place; carry cash for smaller spots.
  • Slurping and lively conversation are fine — it's a relaxed setting.

Finding a good one

Izakaya cluster in nightlife and station areas. Look for busy spots with locals, picture menus, or red lanterns (akachochin) outside, a traditional izakaya marker. Alley districts like Tokyo's Omoide Yokocho are full of tiny, characterful ones. When in doubt, a busy place is usually a good sign.

Bottom line

An evening at an izakaya — sharing small plates, clinking glasses, and soaking up the buzz — is one of the most enjoyable and authentic experiences in Japan. Order a drink, graze through dishes in rounds, pour for your companions, and settle in for a great night.

title: Japanese Drinks Guide: Sake, Beer, Whisky and More
excerpt: From sake to world-class whisky to vending-machine teas, here's a guide to drinking in Japan for first-time visitors.
content:
Japan's drinks are as rich and varied as its food, from traditional sake to award-winning whisky to the ever-present vending-machine teas. Here's a first-timer's guide to what to drink and how.

Sake (nihonshu)

Sake — fermented rice wine — is Japan's signature traditional drink, ranging from dry to sweet, served warm or chilled depending on the type and season. Premium sake is often best cold. It pairs beautifully with Japanese food. Don't be shy about asking staff for a recommendation; there's a sake for every palate. In social settings, it's customary to pour for others rather than yourself.

Beer

Japanese beer is hugely popular and excellent — crisp lagers from the major domestic brands dominate izakaya and restaurants. Order "nama biru" for draft. There's also a growing craft-beer scene in the cities. Beer is the default first drink at most gatherings.

Whisky

Japanese whisky has earned a world-class reputation, with several distilleries winning international acclaim. The hugely popular highball (whisky and soda water over ice) is a refreshing, easy-drinking way to enjoy it and a staple at izakaya. Premium bottles can be pricey and sought-after, but a highball is affordable everywhere.

Shochu

Shochu is a distilled spirit (from barley, sweet potato, rice, and more) that's stronger than sake, often drunk on the rocks, with water, or in a chu-hai. It's deeply popular and worth trying, especially regional varieties.

Chu-hai and cocktails

Chu-hai (shochu highballs, often fruity and canned or on tap) are light, sweet, and popular, including the famous lemon sour. Cocktails are widely available, and Japan has a celebrated, meticulous cocktail-bar culture in its cities.

Non-alcoholic drinks

  • Green tea and matcha: everywhere, hot or cold, often free with meals.
  • Vending machines: on nearly every street, dispensing hot and cold teas, coffees, juices, and water — a daily convenience.
  • Convenience-store coffee: freshly brewed, cheap, and good.
  • Tap water is safe to drink throughout Japan.

Drinking culture and etiquette

  • Start gatherings with a "kanpai!" (cheers).
  • Pour for others, not yourself, and let them refill your glass.
  • Izakaya often offer nomihodai (all-you-can-drink) for a set time and price.
  • The legal drinking age is 20.
  • Public drinking is generally tolerated, but be respectful and never disruptive.
  • No tipping at bars.

Bottom line

Whether you're sipping premium sake with dinner, ordering highball after highball at an izakaya, or just grabbing a cold green tea from a vending machine, Japan's drink culture is a pleasure to explore. Pace yourself, pour for your friends, and toast to a great trip.

title: Food Tours in Japan: Are They Worth It?
excerpt: Food tours can be a great way for first-timers to eat well and learn. Here's what to expect and when a guided food experience is worth booking.
content:
Japan's food scene is incredible but can feel hard to access for first-timers — language barriers, tiny specialist shops, and not knowing where to start. A guided food tour can solve all of that. Here's what to expect and whether one is worth it for you.

Why a food tour can be worth it

  • Access: guides take you to local spots you might never find or feel confident entering alone, including tiny izakaya and hidden gems.
  • Language help: ordering and interacting is handled for you, removing the intimidation factor.
  • Learning: you'll understand what you're eating, the culture behind it, and etiquette — knowledge you carry through the rest of your trip.
  • Variety: tasting many dishes in one outing is a great way to discover favorites early in your trip.
  • Social: a fun, low-stress way to enjoy the food scene, especially solo or for first-timers.

Types of food tours

  • Market tours: exploring places like Tsukiji (Tokyo) or Nishiki (Kyoto) with tastings.
  • Izakaya / bar-hopping tours: an evening sampling small plates and drinks across several pubs.
  • Street-food and neighborhood tours: grazing through districts like Osaka's Dotonbori.
  • Themed tours: focused on ramen, sushi, sake, or sweets.
  • Cooking classes: hands-on experiences making sushi, ramen, or home-style dishes.

When it's most worth it

A food tour is especially valuable early in your trip (to build confidence and learn the ropes), if you're a solo traveler, if you find the language barrier daunting, or if you simply love food and want a deep dive. It's also great for accessing nightlife dining you might not navigate alone.

When you might skip it

If you're an adventurous, independent eater who enjoys discovering places yourself, or you're on a tight budget (tours cost more than eating solo), you may prefer to explore on your own — Japan's photo menus, ticket machines, and konbini make independent eating easy. Many travelers do one tour and then explore solo for the rest of the trip.

Booking tips

  • Book popular tours in advance, especially in peak seasons.
  • Check what's included (number of tastings, drinks, group size).
  • Read recent reviews and choose well-rated operators.
  • Note any dietary restrictions when booking.
  • Come hungry — tours involve a lot of eating.

Bottom line

For first-timers, a food tour early in the trip can be a fantastic investment — unlocking access, easing the language barrier, and teaching you to eat confidently for the rest of your stay. If you love food or feel unsure where to start, it's well worth considering.

title: What to Eat in Osaka: The Nation's Kitchen
excerpt: Osaka is Japan's street-food capital. Here are the must-eat dishes — takoyaki, okonomiyaki, kushikatsu — and where to find them.
content:
Osaka is known as "the nation's kitchen," and eating is the main reason many visit. Its food is hearty, casual, and street-focused, summed up by the local word kuidaore — to eat yourself into ruin. Here's what to eat and where.

Takoyaki

Takoyaki are Osaka's iconic street snack — ball-shaped batter dumplings filled with diced octopus, cooked in special molded pans, then topped with savory sauce, mayo, dried bonito flakes, and seaweed. Watching them being made and eating them hot off the griddle is an essential Osaka experience. Find them all over Dotonbori and the street-food areas.

Okonomiyaki

Okonomiyaki is a savory pancake of batter and shredded cabbage mixed with ingredients like pork, seafood, or cheese, grilled and topped with sauce, mayo, bonito flakes, and seaweed. The name means "grilled as you like it." Osaka-style mixes everything together (versus Hiroshima's layered version). Often cooked on a griddle at your table — fun and filling.

Kushikatsu

Kushikatsu are skewers of meat, seafood, and vegetables, breaded and deep-fried, served with a communal dipping sauce. The golden rule, famously posted in shops: no double-dipping in the shared sauce. They're a specialty of the retro Shinsekai district and a great casual meal.

More Osaka eats

  • Kitsune udon: udon noodles topped with sweet fried tofu, said to have Osaka origins.
  • Yakiniku: grilled meat you cook yourself — Osaka has many great spots.
  • Horumon: grilled offal, a local favorite for the adventurous.
  • Kuromon Market eats: fresh seafood, skewers, and snacks at the famous covered market.

Where to eat

  • Dotonbori: the neon street-food heart — takoyaki, okonomiyaki, and endless eats.
  • Shinsekai: retro district famous for kushikatsu.
  • Kuromon Market: "Osaka's kitchen" market for fresh seafood and stalls.
  • Namba: packed with restaurants of every kind.

Tips

  • Osaka food is best enjoyed casually — graze across multiple stalls and spots.
  • Come hungry and pace yourself across the evening.
  • Remember the no-double-dipping rule for kushikatsu.
  • Carry cash for street stalls; no tipping.

Bottom line

Osaka is a paradise for casual, delicious street food. Make a beeline for Dotonbori, eat takoyaki and okonomiyaki hot off the griddle, try kushikatsu in Shinsekai, and embrace the kuidaore spirit — it's one of Japan's most fun food experiences.
